summary.text: At \(n=473165\), the number \(5292270077783=a(n)+4\) lies strictly between the two proposed endpoints.  It is itself a Sierpiński number: splitting every positive exponent modulo \(48\), congruence computations give a proper divisor of \(5292270077783\cdot2^m+1\) from \(\{3,5,7,17,97,257,673\}\) in every residue class, with periodicity supplied by \(2^{48}\equiv1\) modulo each divisor.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=9{,}454{,}129+11{,}184{,}810n.
\]
Recall that, in the formulation of the conjecture, a natural number \(k\) is a Sierpiński number if it is odd, is greater than \(1\), and \(k2^m+1\) is composite for every positive integer \(m\).

We will disprove the claimed consecutiveness by exhibiting a Sierpiński number strictly between \(a(473165)\) and \(a(473165)+28\). Define
\[
K=5{,}292{,}270{,}077{,}783.
\]
The main point is to prove that \(K\) is a Sierpiński number. We do this with a covering of all exponents by congruence classes.

First note the following elementary periodicity principle. Suppose \(p>1\), \(2^t\equiv1\pmod p\), and \(m\equiv r\pmod t\). Writing \(m=tq+r\), we have
\[
2^m=2^{tq+r}=(2^t)^q2^r\equiv2^r\pmod p.
\]
Consequently, if in addition \(K2^r+1\equiv0\pmod p\), then
\[
p\mid K2^m+1.
\]

The required base congruences and power periods are given by the following table. The first column states the condition on \(m\); the representative \(r\) and period \(t\) used in the periodicity argument are displayed explicitly.

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c}
\text{condition on }m&p&r&t&K\bmod p&2^r\bmod p&2^t\bmod p\\ \hline
m\equiv0\pmod2&3&0&2&2&1&1\\
m\equiv3\pmod4&5&3&4&3&3&1\\
m\equiv1\pmod{12}&7&1&3&3&2&1\\
m\equiv1\pmod8&17&1&8&8&2&1\\
m\equiv5\pmod{16}&257&5&16&8&32&1\\
m\equiv29\pmod{48}&97&29&48&94&65&1\\
m\equiv45\pmod{48}&673&45&48&665&589&1
\end{array}
\]

In the row for \(7\), the hypothesis \(m\equiv1\pmod{12}\) in particular gives \(m\equiv1\pmod3\), which is why period \(3\) suffices.

Here are the arithmetic checks underlying the table. The residues of \(K\) are
\[
\begin{aligned}
K&\equiv2\pmod3,&K&\equiv3\pmod5,&K&\equiv3\pmod7,\\
K&\equiv8\pmod{17},&K&\equiv8\pmod{257},&K&\equiv94\pmod{97},\\
K&\equiv665\pmod{673}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The corresponding products are
\[
\begin{aligned}
2\cdot1+1&=3\equiv0\pmod3,\\
3\cdot3+1&=10\equiv0\pmod5,\\
3\cdot2+1&=7\equiv0\pmod7,\\
8\cdot2+1&=17\equiv0\pmod{17},\\
8\cdot32+1&=257\equiv0\pmod{257},\\
94\cdot65+1&=6111=97\cdot63,\\
665\cdot589+1&=391686=673\cdot582.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus in every row \(K2^r+1\equiv0\pmod p\). The period congruences are also direct:
\[
2^2\equiv1\pmod3,\quad
2^4\equiv1\pmod5,\quad
2^3\equiv1\pmod7,
\]
\[
2^8=256\equiv1\pmod{17},\qquad
2^{16}=65536=257\cdot255+1.
\]
For the last two rows,
\[
2^{48}-1=97\cdot2{,}901{,}803{,}883{,}615
             =673\cdot418{,}239{,}192{,}735,
\]
so \(2^{48}\equiv1\) modulo both \(97\) and \(673\). The base-power reductions in those rows are
\[
2^{29}\equiv65\pmod{97},\qquad
2^{45}\equiv589\pmod{673}.
\]
For example, the exact divisions are
\[
2^{29}=97\cdot5{,}534{,}751+65,
\]
\[
2^{45}=673\cdot52{,}279{,}899{,}091+589.
\]
This establishes all entries used in the table.

It remains to check that the listed congruence conditions cover every exponent \(m\). This can be seen by reducing modulo \(48\). Every even residue is covered by the first row. Among the odd residues, every residue congruent to \(3\pmod4\), namely
\[
3,7,11,15,19,23,27,31,35,39,43,47\pmod{48},
\]
is covered by the second row. The only residues left are therefore
\[
1,5,9,13,17,21,25,29,33,37,41,45\pmod{48}.
\]
They split as follows:

* \(1,13,25,37\pmod{48}\) are all \(1\pmod{12}\), so they are covered by the divisor \(7\).
* \(9,17,33,41\pmod{48}\) are all \(1\pmod8\), so they are covered by the divisor \(17\).
* \(5,21\pmod{48}\) are \(5\pmod{16}\), so they are covered by the divisor \(257\). (The residue \(37\pmod{48}\) also has this property, but it was already covered by \(7\).)
* The remaining residues \(29\) and \(45\pmod{48}\) are covered by \(97\) and \(673\), respectively.

Hence, for every integer \(m\geq0\), at least one of
\[
3,5,7,17,257,97,673
\]
divides \(K2^m+1\). In particular this holds for every positive \(m\), as required in the definition of a Sierpiński number.

Each listed divisor is greater than \(1\). Moreover,
\[
K2^m+1\geq K+1>673
\]
for every \(m\geq0\), so whichever listed number divides \(K2^m+1\) is a proper divisor: it is strictly smaller than \(K2^m+1\). A number possessing a divisor strictly between \(1\) and itself cannot be prime. Thus \(K2^m+1\) is composite for every positive integer \(m\).

Finally, \(K\) is odd (its last digit is \(3\)) and \(K>1\). Together with the preceding covering argument, this proves that \(K\) is a Sierpiński number.

We now locate \(K\) in the sequence interval. Direct calculation gives
\[
11{,}184{,}810\cdot473{,}165=5{,}292{,}260{,}623{,}650,
\]
and hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(473165)
&=9{,}454{,}129+11{,}184{,}810\cdot473{,}165\\
&=5{,}292{,}270{,}077{,}779.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
K=a(473165)+4.
\]
In particular,
\[
a(473165)<K<a(473165)+28,
\]
since \(0<4<28\). Numerically, the full interval comparison is
\[
5{,}292{,}270{,}077{,}779
<5{,}292{,}270{,}077{,}783
<5{,}292{,}270{,}077{,}807.
\]

Thus there is a Sierpiński number \(K\) strictly between \(a(473165)\) and \(a(473165)+28\). Consequently those two numbers are not consecutive Sierpiński numbers. Since the conjecture asserted this consecutiveness for every \(n\geq0\), the single index \(n=473165\) disproves it.
